title: I'm the devil's advocate on the Trump council seeking signs of alien life on earth. Here's why. - The Boston Globe
excerpt: Those videos are not what they may seem.
content:

It is this latter question I have studied for 35 years since founding “Skeptic” magazine, becoming something of an expert on anomalous phenomena, and since July the council has had weekly Zoom meetings to discuss the many videos, photographs, and documents released by the Department of Defense pursuant to a presidential order.

So far, in my opinion, we have found no verifiable evidence of contact with or discovery of extraterrestrial intelligence, although it is striking just how many anomalous phenomena have appeared in our skies (and maybe in our oceans).

Unfortunately, there are significant practical hurdles to our work: The videos we’re working with are filled with redactions in the form of blacked-out rectangles that presumably contain information that would allow us to calculate distance, speed, location, and size of the UAPs.

For instance, as council members Jacob Haqq-Misra and Ravi Kopparapu wrote in an analysis of 112 videos released by the Trump administration, the information provided to the council was not sufficient “to distinguish between a bird flying at close range and a large craft traveling at Mach 5 a kilometer away.”

So until we get more detailed information on these videos, photographs, and documents, I’m putting UAPs in three categories, from most to least likely:

First, there is the category of “ordinary terrestrial” (balloons, camera/lens effects, visual illusions, etc.). Next is “extraordinary terrestrial” (Russian or Chinese spy planes or drones capable of feats of physics and aerodynamics unheard of in the United States). And least likely: “extraordinary extraterrestrial” (alien intelligence).

Let’s take them in order.

Ordinary Terrestrial. As UFOlogist Leslie Kean estimates in her best-selling book “UFOs: Generals, Pilots, and Government Officials Go on the Record,” “Roughly 90 to 95 percent of UFO sightings can be explained” as “weather balloons, flares, sky lanterns, planes flying in formation, secret military aircraft, birds reflecting the sun, planes reflecting the sun, blimps, helicopters, the planets Venus or Mars, meteors or meteorites, space junk, satellites, swamp gas, spinning eddies, sundogs, ball lightning, ice crystals, reflected light off clouds, lights on the ground or lights reflected on a cockpit window.”

When we are confronted, then, with a UAP in the form of a grainy video or blurry photograph, there is a good chance (a 90 to 95 percent probability, in fact) that it is one of these ordinary terrestrial phenomena.

Extraordinary Terrestrial. Could UAPs be superadvanced technology developed by the Chinese, the Russians, or some rogue state or terrorist organization, capable of speeds and turns that seemingly defy all known physics and aerodynamics? Very unlikely. First, if the Russians had such drones, spy planes, or related but as yet unknown (to us) technology, wouldn’t they use it in the Ukraine war? We know the Chinese have spy balloons because we tracked and shot one down over US airspace in 2023, but the technology was more 19th century than 23rd.

Moreover, it defies logic that some nation, corporation, or lone individual — no matter how smart and creative — could have developed an aircraft that is, essentially, centuries ahead of all known present technologies. That is not how innovation works. It would be as if we were still flying biplanes while Russia or China was flying stealth fighter jets, or we were still experimenting with Robert Goddard’s liquid-fuel rockets of the 1920s while they were testing SpaceX-level rocketry. Impossible. Our adversaries would not be able to conceal the advances that led to such technological wizardry.

Extraordinary Extraterrestrial. Although few scientists today believe in miracles, the majority do suspect that there likely is life — maybe even intelligent life — somewhere in the cosmos. This is based on the (literally) astronomically high number of possibilities: The known universe contains hundreds of billions of galaxies, each of which consists of hundreds of billions of stars, and the majority of stars have planets. Astrophysicists estimate that there may be as many as 700 quintillion planets in the universe. If Earth were the only one hosting life, that would be, well, miraculous.

But have aliens come to Earth? That’s a different question. And the evidence collected over three-quarters of a century is just not strong enough to support the claim of contact with or discovery of extraterrestrial intelligence.

That hasn’t dissuaded figures like David Grusch, a former Air Force officer and intelligence official who recently told Joe Rogan that the government is hiding dead reptilian aliens that US soldiers shot (after the reptilians tried to kill said soldiers). The reptilians, Grusch added, are warring with a separate race of gray aliens here on Earth. He went on to suggest that there’s one UFO so large that it can’t be moved, so the government built a giant building around it. And he said there’s an underwater structure the size of many city blocks in an ocean somewhere that houses alien intelligences. Unsurprisingly, when Rogan asked him for details, Grusch clammed up, explaining that he had to protect his sources.

“I know this all sounds completely crazy,” Grusch said. Indeed. Hearing stories like these for over three decades now, and every one of them sounds pretty unbelievable.

That said, I agree with Avi Loeb when he says: “If, after analyzing new data on millions of objects, we will find beyond a reasonable doubt that one of them has a non-human technological origin, that would constitute the biggest scientific discovery ever made by humanity.” And I hope he wins a $1,000 bet I have with him that by Dec. 31, 2030, we will not have made such a discovery. But I will require significant proof. For as the OG alien searcher Carl Sagan famously said in his 1980 PBS “Cosmos” series in the episode on extraterrestrial intelligences: “Extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence.”

Will the UAP Science Advisory Council (or some other organization or individual) reach that level of certainty? If I did not believe it was possible, I would not be serving on the council. But I do agree with skeptical scientists (that is, most of them) that we need much more data from the government (if they have it) than they’ve been giving us. On this, the devil’s advocates and those who are curious about dead reptilian aliens can agree. I hope the powers that be at long last disclose what the government really knows about life from the beyond.
